excerpt: Carpal tunnel can qualify for workers' comp in Georgia and South Carolina as a repetitive work injury. How to prove it is work-related, and when to report it.
keyTakeaways: Carpal tunnel syndrome can qualify for workers' compensation in both Georgia and South Carolina as a repetitive work injury — South Carolina requires medical evidence of the work link (S.C. Code § 42-1-172). Georgia requires reporting within 30 days (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-80) and filing within one year of the injury, with extensions after employer-paid treatment or income benefits (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-82). South Carolina allows 90 days to report and two years to file, both measured from when you knew or should have known your carpal tunnel was work-related and compensable, with a seven-year outer limit for filing (S.C. Code §§ 42-15-20, 42-15-40). Workers' comp is no-fault — carelessness does not bar a claim, and work that aggravates a pre-existing condition can still be covered.

faqs.question: Can I get workers' comp for carpal tunnel syndrome?
faqs.answer: Yes. Both Georgia and South Carolina cover carpal tunnel syndrome as a repetitive work injury under their workers' compensation systems when the condition arises out of and in the course of employment. You must establish a causal connection between your work duties and the development of CTS; South Carolina requires a doctor's opinion, to a reasonable degree of medical certainty, linking it to your job (S.C. Code § 42-1-172).

faqs.question: How do I prove my carpal tunnel is work-related?
faqs.answer: You need medical evidence from a doctor linking your CTS to your work duties, documentation of the repetitive hand and wrist movements your job requires, nerve conduction studies confirming the diagnosis, and a timeline showing your symptoms developed during the period of repetitive work.

faqs.question: What is the deadline to report carpal tunnel to my employer?
faqs.answer: In Georgia, you must report within 30 days of the injury (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-80); for carpal tunnel that builds up over time, report as soon as you suspect your job is the cause rather than waiting for a diagnosis. In South Carolina, the reporting deadline is 90 days under S.C. Code § 42-15-20, measured from when you knew or should have known your condition was work-related and compensable.

faqs.question: What benefits can I receive for work-related carpal tunnel?
faqs.answer: Benefits include authorized medical treatment (doctor visits, therapy, surgery), temporary total disability (two-thirds of your average weekly wage, up to $800 a week in Georgia for injuries on or after July 1, 2023, and $1,189.94 in South Carolina for 2026 accidents) or partial disability (two-thirds of the wage difference), and permanent partial disability compensation if you have lasting impairment. Vocational rehabilitation is a Georgia comp benefit only for catastrophic injuries and is not part of South Carolina's system.

faqs.question: Can my employer deny my carpal tunnel claim because I have a pre-existing condition?
faqs.answer: Having a pre-existing condition does not automatically disqualify your claim. If your work duties aggravated, accelerated, or worsened a pre-existing carpal tunnel condition, you may still be entitled to workers' compensation benefits in both Georgia and South Carolina if a doctor connects the worsening to your job (O.C.G.A. § 34-9-1(4); S.C. Code § 42-9-35).

faqs.question: How long is recovery from carpal tunnel release surgery?
faqs.answer: Recovery from carpal tunnel surgery typically takes several weeks to several months. Your surgeon sets your return-to-work date; grip and pinch strength usually return in about 2 to 3 months, but can take 6 to 12 months if the nerve was badly compressed. Workers' compensation covers authorized medical treatment and provides disability benefits during recovery.
